It is not about being perfect. It is about showing that you have the base skills to grow once classes begin. A good nursing program entrance test gives schools a complete picture of your readiness and positions you for success.

cards.title: Inside The Exam Format
content: Most versions of a nursing admission test follow a familiar layout. Whether your program uses TEAS, HESI A2, or another nursing test name, the structure usually includes reading, science, math, and English sections. The pacing can feel a little fast, and that is intentional because nursing programs move quickly too. These exams give you a preview of that rhythm.

The reading questions may feel heavier than expected. The math may require careful attention to units and details. The science often pulls from human anatomy, basic chemistry, and general physiology. None of it is designed to confuse you, but you do need to stay focused. Students often say the most surprising part is how mentally draining the exam feels, even when the content is familiar. It is a blend of timing, pressure, and the knowledge that this exam is part of the test to get into nursing school. A good nursing program entrance test helps schools understand your academic foundation and shows you the type of thinking nursing classes will require.

A nursing entrance examination does more than give a score. It reveals how you think under pressure and where your strengths naturally appear. Maybe your reading speed is strong, but scientific reasoning needs a refresh. Maybe math comes easily, but you lose time when the clock starts. The exam helps you understand these patterns long before you step into a classroom.

Students often notice habits during their practice tests that they never realized they had, such as rushing through reading questions or second guessing answers that were correct the first time. This kind of insight is valuable. Schools rely on these exams because they show readiness, but the real benefit goes to the student. When you understand your strongest areas and your weaker ones, the start of nursing school becomes smoother and significantly less stressful. This is why many programs treat it as a core nursing program admissions exam requirement.

questions.question: Should I take the TEAS or HESI
paragraphs: Choosing between TEAS and HESI usually depends on the school more than the student. Most programs already list which exam they accept, so your choice is often made for you. Still, people talk about the feel of each exam in slightly different ways. TEAS usually feels a little more balanced across reading, science, math, and English, and many students say the timing feels fair once you settle in. HESI, from what most students describe, has a sharper focus on vocabulary and anatomy. If you have a stronger science background, HESI tends to feel familiar. If you like a smoother mix of subjects, TEAS might feel more natural. Truth is, both tests are used to check whether you are ready for nursing school. So it often comes down to which exam your program requires and which format fits the way your brain likes to work when pressure starts creeping in.

The HESI exam is something students hear about early, especially if their program uses it to screen applicants. It is a long look at how prepared you are for the academic side of nursing. The exam covers reading, vocabulary, grammar, math, and a science section that can include anatomy and basic physiology. People often describe it as a bit more detailed than they expected, especially in the vocabulary area. It feels similar to a college placement test, in the way it checks your ability to reason through questions calmly. Schools rely on the HESI because it shows whether someone can manage the pace of nursing classes. You might notice the exam rewards students who take time to practice rather than hoping natural ability will carry them. When you walk in with a clear head and steady preparation, the test becomes less intimidating and more like a checkpoint in your journey.

What is a good score on a nursing entrance exam
paragraphs: A good score depends on the school and the exam. Some programs want mid seventies on TEAS, others prefer eighties or higher, and certain schools have competitive ranges that feel intense. But from the conversations you hear in study groups, a strong score is usually the one that gives you choices. A score that does not leave you worrying whether your application looks weak. Students often remember the feeling more than the number, that moment when the score pops up and your shoulders drop a little. What matters most is that your score shows you understand the basics and can handle the material that is coming. A good score on a nursing entrance examination is one that reflects steady effort and real understanding, not rushed cramming. It tells the school that you are ready for the challenge and tells you that the dream is actually within reach.

questions.question: Is nursing has an entrance exam
paragraphs: Most nursing programs do. Not all, but a surprising number of them require a nursing entrance exam before they make admission decisions. Schools use it to see how prepared you are for the pace of nursing school, especially in subjects like reading comprehension and science reasoning. Students often feel nervous before taking the exam because it becomes the first moment where the journey feels real. It is not a barrier meant to discourage you. It is more like a snapshot that helps schools place students who can succeed once the work begins. If your program requires one, it will usually list TEAS or HESI as the exam of choice. If it does not require an exam, you might notice the application weighs other areas more heavily, like GPA or interviews. In most cases, though, yes, there is an exam somewhere in the process.

questions.question: Is the nursing exam difficult
paragraphs: It can feel difficult if you walk in without preparation, and surprisingly manageable if you give yourself time to study. Students often compare the exam to high school science mixed with a little college level reading. The challenge is not usually the content. It is the timing. The nerves. The moment you realize you cannot sit and stare at a question forever. Some students say the reading feels heavier than expected. Others say the science questions pull up memories they forgot they had from biology classes. The exam checks how well you think under pressure. That is why people describe it differently. Some find it comfortable, others feel overwhelmed at first. With consistent practice, steady pacing, and realistic questions, the nursing school test becomes much less intimidating. It starts to feel like something you can handle with calm focus.

Most students hear two names more than anything else. TEAS and HESI. These are the most common exams used by programs across the country. Some schools simply call it the nursing entry exam or the test to get into nursing school. But TEAS and HESI are the main ones students prepare for. TEAS covers reading, science, math, and English. HESI includes vocabulary, grammar, reading, math, and a more detailed science section. The name your school uses depends on the system they trust to measure readiness. No matter the label, the purpose is the same. Schools want to understand whether you are ready for the pace of nursing classes and whether your study habits line up with the demands of the profession. Students usually learn the name of the exam early in the application process, often right after talking with an advisor.
questions.question: What is the nursing school entrance exam called
Do all nursing schools require entrance exams
paragraphs: Not every school requires an exam, but most programs do. It is something you notice when you start comparing application pages. Some community colleges do not require a nursing program test, while many universities rely heavily on TEAS or HESI. The exam gives schools a common way to measure readiness across students from different backgrounds. Without it, they rely more on GPA or previous coursework. Students who apply to programs that do require an exam often feel more prepared once classes begin because the study process forces them to review reading and science concepts that show up again later. Programs that skip the exam usually have other requirements like interviews or strict GPA cutoffs. It depends on the school. But in most cases, expect to take an exam somewhere along the way.

questions.question: How can I prepare for a nursing entrance exam
paragraphs: Preparing for the nursing admission test feels less overwhelming when you break it into small daily tasks. Students often start with short sessions, maybe twenty or thirty minutes, then build up as the exam gets closer. Reading practice is huge because many questions rely on careful interpretation. Science needs slow, steady review and not rushed cramming. Math benefits from repetition. You might notice that realistic practice questions help the most. They give you a feel for timing and the flow of the exam. Some students like studying late at night when everything is quiet. Others prefer early morning when their mind feels clear. What matters is consistency and understanding where you tend to lose time or confidence. When you prepare in a way that feels natural and honest, the exam becomes less intimidating and much more manageable.

cards.title: Clinical Judgment Pathways
content: ATI and HESI both love to build questions that move in steps, almost like watching a patient scenario unfold in slow motion. You read a little, pause, reread a few lines, and suddenly realize what the question is really about. These pathway questions usually follow the same pattern your clinical instructors drilled into you: recognize the vital cue, decide what it means, choose the safest response, and then evaluate whether the plan worked. Many students say these questions are where anxiety kicks in because the answer options can look so similar. But once you understand that the exam is trying to see whether you can think through a situation the way a new nurse would, the process becomes clearer. ATI uses these pathways to mirror the NCLEX style of reasoning, while HESI blends it with slightly trickier wording. Both are looking for the same thing though: whether you can think safely and consistently under quiet pressure.

HESI is almost famous for these. They love the unstable patient, the unexpected shift in labs, or the vague complaint that makes your stomach clench for a second. ATI includes them too, but HESI tends to make the red flags a little softer, so you have to look closer. These questions place you in situations where small choices carry big consequences. Maybe the postpartum patient describing a strange pain, the cardiac patient with a sudden change in rhythm, or a child whose breathing pattern shifts in ways you cannot ignore. These scenarios matter because they show how quickly you can spot danger and respond with the safest option. Students often talk about the feeling of holding their breath for a moment before choosing an answer. That is normal. These questions measure your readiness in the moments that count most.

sections.content: There is something steadying about knowing your study habits are grounded in research instead of panic. Students preparing for the RN nursing exit exam or the LPN nursing exit exam quickly notice that what worked earlier in the program does not always work here. The questions are heavier now, and ATI and HESI both expect deeper clinical reasoning. That is why spaced repetition, short reviews, and case based study sessions start to feel more natural the closer you get to the test. Your brain retains information better when you revisit it gently rather than forcing it through long marathon sessions. You might catch yourself remembering things you thought you forgot, almost like the knowledge rises back to the surface on its own. RN students often share how this method helped them with med surg priorities, while LPN students say it made their pharmacology review less overwhelming. Evidence centered studying lets your understanding settle in slowly, and that makes the nursing exit exam feel less like something that wants to catch you off guard.
sections.title: Evidence Based Study Methods
Performance Tracking Routine
sections.content: Many students reach the point where they feel like they are studying constantly but can’t tell if they are improving. That’s where tracking your performance becomes a small lifesaver. ATI and HESI rationales reveal a lot about your thinking, and both RN and LPN students benefit differently from this kind of reflection. RN students often realize they rush through pathophysiology clues and need more time with labs and prioritization. LPN students frequently find that medication questions or subtle safety scenarios need slow, careful review. When you mark your weak spots, you begin to see the test more clearly. Some keep a simple notebook. Others use digital trackers. What matters is noticing what keeps tripping you up and watching those areas shrink over time. When this happens, the exam stops feeling unpredictable. It becomes a pattern you can navigate instead of hoping for luck.

To be honest, mindset becomes just as important as content at this stage. Both RN and LPN students walk into their exit exams carrying the weight of their entire program. You might feel the same nerves you felt before your TEAS or your very first nursing program test. What helps is learning to steady your mind so your reasoning stays clear. Students who practice short breathing sessions or quiet resets between practice questions usually perform better when it counts. RN students say this calmness helps during complex case scenarios. LPN students say it helps during tasks involving pattern recognition and safe decision making. A calm mind notices details an anxious mind misses. On exam day, that matters. Mindset training builds a kind of quiet confidence, the kind that makes the entire exam feel doable rather than overwhelming.
sections.title: Exit Exam Mindset Training

sections.content: From what I have seen, the biggest improvement for both RN and LPN students comes when they stop reviewing random content and start reviewing by competency. ATI and HESI exams don’t care whether you memorized ten more pages. They care whether you can provide safe care. RN exams lean harder into complex med surg situations, cardiac rhythms, leadership and delegation, and broader clinical judgment. LPN exit exams usually emphasize stable versus unstable patients, focused assessments, medication safety, and knowing when to report something to the RN. When you study by competency, you start recognizing these patterns instead of drowning in extra information. You might even notice gaps you didn’t realize were there. Maybe postpartum care needs another look. Or you realize your delegation rules are fuzzy. Reviewing this way not only prepares you for the exam but helps your brain work the way ATI and HESI want you to think. It is a calmer, clearer way to study.
sections.title: Competency Focused Review

cards.title: Exam Purpose
content: The goal of a nursing exit exam is not to trick you or make you feel small. It is there to check whether your thinking lines up with safe practice. You might notice the questions feel familiar, almost like a blend of school quizzes and the tougher, case based items instructors loved throwing at you. These exams carry the same rhythm as NCLEX style reasoning. A patient situation, a few clues, and the request for your next best action. It is meant to measure your readiness, not perfection. Many students say the exam feels like a quiet conversation between all the things you learned and what you can do under a little pressure. It touches everything from med surg to mental health, and most of the time, the challenge is pacing yourself so you do not burn out midway. The purpose is safety and confidence. Nothing more complicated than that.

On the actual day, the testing room tends to have this stillness that makes you more aware of your own breathing. It reminds some students of the TEAS Reading section where the room felt too quiet and your pencil suddenly felt louder than it needed to be. You start with simple questions, then the cases gradually stretch your decision making. Some questions feel clear, others feel messy, and a few might make you close your eyes for a second just to reset. That is normal. The test mirrors real nursing life, where you are expected to pick out the important detail and trust your training even when you feel unsure. You will see labs to interpret, symptoms to prioritize, and patient cues that guide your next step. The experience is steady, sometimes draining, but almost always fair.

How hard is a nursing exit exam?
paragraphs: Hard means something different depending on who you ask. If you talk to students right after clinicals, many will say the exit exam feels like a long day of taking care of imaginary patients. Others say it feels harder than expected because the questions test your instincts more than your memory. The ATI and HESI versions both try to see how you think when the clues are subtle and the answers look almost identical. RN students often mention the difficulty of choosing the safest action when everything feels urgent. LPN students talk about how pharmacology and safety questions can sometimes shake their confidence. But to be honest, once you understand how these exams frame their questions, the difficulty becomes manageable. It feels less like a trap and more like a thoughtful check that you are ready for real practice. Hard, yes. Impossible, no.

If you ask around, the answers will wander a bit. Some people swear the NCLEX is the toughest. Others say the HESI Exit Exam is harder because it feels unpredictable in the moment. The ATI version can feel intense too, especially when the rationales force you to confront habits you didn’t realize you had. Many RN students mention that the hardest part is the mental load more than the content. You sit there trying to keep calm while the clock keeps moving. LPN students often say the pharmacology section feels rough because it expects quick recognition more than memorized facts. Truth is, the “hardest” exam depends on where you feel less steady. Some students struggle with clinical judgment questions, others freeze up when labs shift suddenly in a scenario. Each exam has its own flavor, but the challenge usually comes from the pressure, not the material itself.

LPN programs use similar tools but tend to focus more on stable care, communication, and safe medication practices. Students often describe this final exam as a moment where everything from the program seems to blend together. You see bits of med surg, maternal newborn care, mental health, pediatrics, and pharmacology woven into patient stories. It is not meant to scare you. It is meant to reflect the thinking you will use as a nurse. In its own way, it is like a rehearsal before stepping into the profession. A quiet but defining moment.

questions.question: What is harder, HESI exit exam or ATI exit exam?
paragraphs: Funny thing is, students rarely agree on this. Some say the HESI Exit Exam feels harder because the questions feel vague at first glance, almost like the exam wants you to slow down and think deeper. Others say ATI feels tougher because it tests your weaknesses with surprising accuracy. RN students often lean toward saying HESI is trickier, probably because it demands sharper clinical judgment when the clues are subtle. LPN students sometimes find ATI harder, especially when medication safety shows up repeatedly. Both exams pull from similar core concepts, and both are designed to challenge your reasoning more than your recall. The real answer depends on how your brain works under pressure. If you think slowly and methodically, ATI might feel smoother. If you think fast and adjust quickly, HESI might feel more natural. They are different kinds of difficult.

The technical final exam for nurses is the NCLEX, but the last test inside nursing school is usually the ATI or HESI exit exam. RN students take the RN versions, LPN students the LPN versions, each focusing on the level of care you are preparing to give. The funny thing is, the exit exam sometimes feels more stressful because you are still juggling graduation requirements, clinical hours, and whatever personal responsibilities life has thrown your way. The NCLEX feels like a mountain, but the exit exam feels like a doorway you must walk through to even reach that mountain. It checks whether you can think safely, prioritize effectively, and keep your head steady during uncertainty. Once you get through it, the NCLEX feels more familiar, like something you have already trained for without realizing it.

What is the hardest class to pass in nursing school?
paragraphs: If you sit down with a group of nursing students, the conversation almost always circles around med surg. Something about the pace, the amount of content, and the way instructors expect you to think several steps ahead makes it feel like a constant uphill climb. Pharmacology is another class that makes students groan, especially when dosage calculations come up at the end of a long clinical week. Some say mental health was surprisingly tough because the questions tested interpretation rather than memorization. Others mention maternal newborn because of all the tiny details that matter. The truth is, the hardest class is usually the one where your foundation is shaky. Once you settle into a rhythm and figure out how to study smarter, the load becomes doable. Still heavy, but not impossible.

questions.question: What are the nursing exit exams called?

RN programs use the RN versions, which lean heavily into complex clinical scenarios and higher level prioritization. LPN programs use the LPN versions, which focus more on stable assignments, basic pharmacology, communication, and safe decision making. Some schools use both as part of their nursing program test structure. These exams are often called readiness exams, predictor exams, or simply “the exit.” The names might shift from campus to campus, but the purpose stays the same: making sure you can think like a nurse before stepping into the NCLEX world. Once you understand how ATI and HESI style their questions, the fear softens a bit, and the entire process feels more predictable.

cards.title: Core Nursing Fundamentals
content: When you look at fundamentals questions, you can almost feel how much the basics shape everything else in nursing school. These questions dip into infection control, basic care, documentation, vital signs, and the familiar nursing process that instructors talk about from day one. You will see items that seem simple at first, something like identifying an abnormal pulse or choosing the correct isolation precautions. Then you realize the test is really checking whether you understand the bigger picture. Students who practice these questions start building a steady internal checklist. They also learn how tiny details in the stem help them rule out answers that do not fit. The benefit is pretty immediate because fundamentals show up in every nursing exam name you can think of. When you are preparing for a test to get into nursing school or reviewing for your next nursing program test, knowing these basics can give you a calm and grounded starting point.

The funny thing about clinical scenario questions is that they feel so real that many students catch themselves imagining an actual patient room. These items blend pharmacology, interventions, prioritization, and delegation all in one moment. You read the stem, pause for a second, and think through the safest action. That pause is where your critical thinking grows. Practicing these scenarios helps you stay steady when a question feels overwhelming. You get better at sorting through symptoms, making sense of medications, and choosing who to help first. These questions prepare you for real nursing exams and for the emotional side of test taking. You learn to manage uncertainty without panicking. Students who work through these types of questions often say that clinical content becomes less intimidating and more like something they can actually handle.

nursing-entrance-exam.bodyContent:
Official ATI TEAS 7 Facts to Keep Straight

The official ATI TEAS Version 7 exam has 170 total questions: 150 scored questions and 20 unscored pretest questions. The full exam time is 209 minutes across four timed sections.

Detail

Value

Total questions

170

Scored questions

150

Unscored pretest questions

20

Total time

209 minutes

Reading

45 total questions; 39 scored; 6 unscored; 55 minutes

Mathematics

38 total questions; 34 scored; 4 unscored; 57 minutes

Science

50 total questions; 44 scored; 6 unscored; 60 minutes

English and Language Usage

37 total questions; 33 scored; 4 unscored; 37 minutes

These are official exam facts. NursingMocks practice sets help you prepare for the skills tested on the exam, but they are not official ATI questions and should not be described as the real exam.

How NursingMocks Fits Into Your TEAS Prep

NursingMocks is an independent nursing exam preparation platform. It is not ATI, is not endorsed by ATI, and does not claim authorization from ATI.

Use it as a practice workspace. The parent ATI TEAS page helps you pick a direction. The subject pages narrow that direction. The set pages are where you answer questions and review the result.

The Four TEAS Sections Do Not Test You the Same Way

Reading

Reading is about proof. An answer can sound sensible and still be wrong if the passage, direction, chart, table, or visual does not support it.

Be careful with words like NOT, EXCEPT, LEAST, and BEST. They change the job of the question. Also, do not reread an entire passage every time you get stuck. Go back to the sentence, paragraph, label, or visual that actually relates to the question.

Math

Math is not just calculation. Many missed questions begin with a bad setup: solving for the wrong value, skipping a unit conversion, or turning the word problem into the wrong equation.

Before you calculate, ask what the question is asking for. Then check the units. That small pause can save more time than rushing into arithmetic and fixing it later.

Science

Science covers Human Anatomy and Physiology, Biology, Chemistry, and Scientific Reasoning. Human Anatomy and Physiology has the largest scored share, but repeated misses in biology, chemistry, or reasoning still matter.

A Science miss usually falls into one of four buckets: you did not know the concept, you knew the facts but missed the relationship, you misread the prompt, or you did not interpret the evidence correctly.

English and Language Usage

English and Language Usage is not only grammar. It also includes language clarity, paragraph organization, using language and vocabulary to express ideas in writing, and revision.

Short questions are easy to underestimate. One comma, verb form, modifier, or word choice can change the answer. Slow down enough to see what the sentence is actually doing.

Full Practice or Subject Practice?

Use subject practice when you need focused work on one section, such as Math setup, Reading evidence, Science concepts, or English conventions. Use full practice when you want to check pacing, stamina, and how well you move across all four sections.

Early in preparation, subject practice usually shows what is breaking. Later, full practice is useful because it shows whether those fixes hold up when the sections are combined.

Question Formats Are Not the Only Difference

ATI TEAS Version 7 uses multiple-choice and alternate item formats across the exam, including multiple select, fill in the blank, ordered response, and hot spot. NursingMocks formats can vary by set, so use the details shown on the set you choose.

Reading: Where is the support?

Math: What is the setup?

Science: Which concept, relationship, or evidence applies?

English: Which version is clearest, most correct, or best organized?

That is why switching sections can feel awkward even when the questions look simple. The subject changes the way you have to think.

Use Results Like a Map

Do not stop at the percentage score. It is useful, but it is too blunt by itself.

In Reading, check whether the answer was directly supported by the passage, source, chart, table, or visual. In Math, separate setup errors from calculation, unit, and interpretation errors. In Science, decide whether the miss came from knowledge, relationships, prompt reading, or evidence. In English, look for convention, meaning, audience-and-purpose, or revision errors.

Then choose the next practice activity from the pattern. Not the subject you like most. Not the section that feels easiest. The pattern.

Timing Needs a Different Plan for Each Section

The official timing gives you a useful frame, but one pacing rule will not fit the whole exam.

Reading time disappears when you reread too much. Math time disappears when the setup is weak. Science time disappears when a scenario or data display takes longer than expected. English time disappears when two answer choices look almost the same.

When you review a timed set, ask where the delay started. That answer is more useful than simply telling yourself to go faster.

The NursingMocks ATI TEAS Reading Practice Test is subject-level practice for students preparing for the Reading part of the ATI TEAS. It lets you work on Reading questions without switching into Math, Science, or English and Language Usage.

This is not the official ATI TEAS exam, and NursingMocks does not provide official ATI questions. It is an independent practice resource for building the Reading habits the exam demands: understanding passages, following written directions, finding evidence, interpreting structure, and using visuals when they appear.

As you practice, read the source first, answer the question, then check the correct response and explanation when one is provided. Keep coming back to one rule: choose the answer the passage, prompt, chart, table, or other source can support.

What Topics Are Covered?

ATI TEAS Reading practice should cover three official Reading areas: Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. Think of them this way: what the source says, how the source is written, and how evidence connects across a passage, chart, table, or other source.

Key Ideas and Details Practice Questions

Key Ideas and Details questions focus on information stated or strongly supported in the source. You may need to find the central idea, choose the best summary, locate a specific detail, follow written directions, understand sequence, or draw a conclusion that stays inside the text.

Small wording matters here. If the prompt asks for the best summary, a true detail may still be too narrow. If it asks what the passage implies, the answer must still be supported by the passage, not by what you already know outside it.

Craft and Structure Practice Questions

Craft and Structure questions look at how the text is built. That can include word meaning in context, author purpose, point of view, tone, organization, and the way a sentence or paragraph affects meaning.

Do not answer these questions from the topic alone. A passage about a serious subject is not automatically angry, biased, or persuasive. Look at the wording. The correct answer should match how the author writes, not just what the passage is about.

Integration of Knowledge and Ideas Practice Questions

Integration of Knowledge and Ideas questions ask you to connect information. You may compare two parts of a text, evaluate a claim, choose the evidence that best supports a conclusion, or combine a passage with a chart, table, label, or other visual.

These questions can feel slower because the answer may not sit in one sentence. You might need to check two details, compare a statement with a visual, or decide which evidence is relevant and which is only related. Related is not enough. The answer has to support the conclusion the question is asking for.

ATI TEAS Reading Question Presentation and Problem Styles

ATI TEAS Reading questions may use passages, written directions, labels, informational text, charts, tables, or other sources. The setup can change, but the job stays the same: read what you are given and choose the answer that fits it best.

The format is only how you submit the answer. The Reading task is the real issue. Are you finding a detail? Choosing a summary? Working out a word from context? Identifying the author's purpose? Comparing a passage with a visual?

On NursingMocks, treat each Reading question like a source check. Before you choose, ask: where is the proof? If you cannot point to support in the passage, prompt, chart, or table, the answer may only sound right.

How Reading Practice Works on NursingMocks

Start by choosing a Reading set from the available NursingMocks practice options. Open the set, read the passage, directions, prompt, or visual source, then answer from what is provided.

After answering, check the correct response and review the explanation when one is included. Pay extra attention when you guessed or narrowed the choices down to two. That is where many Reading mistakes become visible.

A missed Reading question is not always a reading problem. Sometimes you found the right paragraph but missed one qualifier. Sometimes you understood the passage but chose an answer that went too far. Use each completed set to spot those patterns before moving to the next one.

Timed ATI TEAS Reading Practice

The official ATI TEAS Reading section gives you 55 minutes for 45 questions. That averages about 1 minute and 13 seconds per question, but Reading timing is not that neat.

A longer passage may take more time upfront, then let you answer several related questions faster. A short question can still slow you down if two answers look close. Treat the average as a pacing guide, not a rule for every item.

Use timed practice to find out where time is disappearing. Maybe you are rereading the full passage for every question. Maybe you are searching too long for one detail. Maybe you keep getting stuck between two answer choices that both sound true.

One practical fix: return to the relevant sentence, paragraph, label, chart, or table when possible. Do not reread everything unless you truly lost the thread. Slow down for words like NOT, EXCEPT, LEAST, MOST, and BEST. They can change the whole question.

Review Your Reading Answers, Explanations, and Results

After a Reading set, do more than check the score. Review the questions you missed, guessed, or answered slowly, then group the mistake by cause.

Error type

What it means

What to check next

Retrieval error

You overlooked an explicit detail, direction, sequence, or qualifier, or searched the wrong part of the source.

Go back to the exact sentence, paragraph, label, chart, or table that supports the answer.

Inference error

You chose a conclusion that went beyond what the source supported.

Separate what the text actually says from what may be true outside the passage.

Craft-and-structure error

You misunderstood the author's purpose, point of view, word choice, tone, or organization.

Look at how the author writes, not only what the topic is about.

Integration error

You did not correctly combine information from different parts of a text, multiple sources, or text and visuals.

Compare the relevant pieces of information side by side before choosing.

 

This is where Reading practice starts to pay off. If retrieval questions keep catching you, slow down and locate the proof. If inference errors keep showing up, stop choosing answers that sound reasonable but are not supported. If integration is the problem, practice moving between a passage and a visual without losing the question's focus.

ATI TEAS Math Section at a Glance

The ATI TEAS Math section has 38 questions and a 57-minute time limit. It includes two scored sub-content areas: Numbers and Algebra, and Measurement and Data.

A balanced practice plan should cover both calculation fluency and real problem setup. The calculator can help with arithmetic, but it cannot choose the equation for you.

What Is the NursingMocks ATI TEAS Math Practice Test?

The NursingMocks ATI TEAS Math practice test is a helpful tool for students getting ready to take the nursing entrance exam, especially when it comes to the Math part. This practice test is not the actual ATI TEAS exam, but rather a way to prepare for it. It also does not take the place of the real test that you will schedule through ATI or your school.

You can use it to work on whole-number and rational-number operations, algebra setup, measurement, unit conversions, geometric quantities, data interpretation, and word problems. When you get a Math question wrong, it is not always because you do not know the math. Sometimes the mistake happens before you even start doing the math. You need to get the setup right before you can solve the problem.

What Topics Are Covered?

The ATI TEAS Math section includes two official sub-content areas: Numbers and Algebra, and Measurement and Data. NursingMocks helps you practice Math by focusing on these same areas, so you can see which types of problems you need to work on.

Numbers and Algebra Practice Questions

Numbers and Algebra practice focuses on whole-number and rational-number operations, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, proportions, expressions, equations, and word problems. Many misses come from setting up the wrong relationship, not from the final arithmetic.

Measurement and Data Practice Questions

Measurement and Data practice focuses on unit conversions, area, perimeter, volume, geometric quantities, charts, graphs, tables, data comparison, and interpretation. Units are a clue. If the answer asks for square units, volume, rate, or percentage, the unit often tells you what kind of setup is needed.

ATI TEAS Math Question Presentation and Problem Styles

The way questions are asked can be different in each NursingMocks Math set, but what really matters is what kind of math problem you are trying to solve.

When you are faced with a Math problem, you might need to solve an equation, turn a word problem into numbers, compare quantities, understand what a table is telling you, read a chart, or pick the right unit to use. Before you start doing any math, take a moment to think about what the question is actually asking for.

How Math Practice Works on NursingMocks

To begin, pick a Math set from the ATI TEAS practice area. Read the question slowly, figure out what it is asking for, set up the problem, and then do the math. After you choose an answer, check whether it is right and compare it to how you set up the problem. This helps you understand where you might have gone wrong.

When an explanation is provided, look for the first place your work split from the correct method. That is usually more useful than only checking the final number.

Use each completed set to decide what to practice next. Repeated missed patterns matter more than one bad question.

Timed ATI TEAS Math Practice

The Math section gives you 57 minutes to answer 38 questions, which averages about 90 seconds for each one. Some questions are quick and just need a simple calculation, but word problems, conversions, and data questions can take longer.

Math pacing usually breaks down in the setup. If you rush the setup, the calculator can give you a precise answer to the wrong problem. Estimate when it helps you catch an unreasonable result.

After a timed set, check where time went: rereading the question, choosing the operation, converting units, or recalculating because the first answer looked wrong.

Review Your Math Answers, Explanations, and Results

When you are done with a Math set, take a closer look at the questions that gave you trouble, the ones you had to guess at, or the ones that took you a while to answer. Usually, the Math questions you miss can be grouped into a few main categories.

  • Setup error: You chose the wrong operation, equation, proportion, or relationship.

  • Calculation error: The setup was right, but the arithmetic or calculator entry was wrong.

  • Unit error: You missed a conversion, label, rate, area, volume, or percentage relationship.

  • Question-reading error: You solved for something different from what the question asked.

Do not treat all wrong answers the same. If the setup was wrong, doing more arithmetic drills will not fix the real problem. Use the most common error type to choose your next Math set or topic review.

ATI TEAS Science Section at a Glance

The official ATI TEAS Science section gives you 60 minutes for 50 questions. Of those, 44 are scored and 6 are unscored pretest questions.

Science section detail

Value

Total questions

50

Scored questions

44

Unscored pretest questions

6

Time limit

60 minutes

Human Anatomy and Physiology

18 scored questions

Biology

9 scored questions

Chemistry

8 scored questions

Scientific Reasoning

9 scored questions

Human Anatomy and Physiology has the largest scored share, so it should not be treated lightly. Still, Science is not only A&P. Biology, Chemistry, and Scientific Reasoning each test a different kind of thinking.

What Is the NursingMocks ATI TEAS Science Practice Test?

The NursingMocks ATI TEAS Science Practice Test is a subject-focused practice page for students preparing for the Science section of the ATI TEAS exam. It is an independent practice resource, not the official ATI TEAS exam, and it does not provide official ATI questions.

Use it when Science feels too broad to review in one sitting. A focused set helps you see whether you need more content review, more practice with relationships between ideas, or more careful reading of scenarios and data.

What Topics Are Covered on ATI TEAS Science?

ATI TEAS Science is organized around Human Anatomy and Physiology, Biology, Chemistry, and Scientific Reasoning. Those areas overlap at times, but they do not ask for the same study habit.

For practice, separate the work. A body-system question may reward accurate recall. A Scientific Reasoning question may reward evidence checking. A Chemistry question may turn on one word in the prompt.

Human Anatomy and Physiology Practice Questions

Human Anatomy and Physiology questions focus on how the body is organized and how major systems work. Practice may involve systems such as cardiovascular, respiratory, nervous, digestive, endocrine, immune, urinary, reproductive, integumentary, or musculoskeletal systems.

The common trap is treating A&P as a list of parts. Many questions care about function and connection: what a structure does, how a process changes, or how one system affects another.

Biology Practice Questions

Biology questions focus on living systems, cellular processes, biological organization, heredity, genetics, and the use of genetic information. These questions often ask you to connect a process with its purpose.

Read direction words carefully. Before, after, increases, decreases, produces, and results in can change the answer. If the relationship is backward, the answer can sound familiar and still be wrong.

Chemistry Practice Questions

Chemistry practice covers properties and changes of matter, bonds, reactions, solutions, acids and bases, and basic chemical relationships. The goal is not to turn this page into a chemistry course. The goal is to practise the decisions that show up in Science questions.

When reviewing Chemistry misses, ask whether you missed the concept or the wording. Product, reactant, opposite, best comparison, acid, base, solution, and concentration are small words with real consequences.

Scientific Reasoning Practice Questions

Scientific Reasoning questions test how you use evidence. You may need to identify variables, interpret observations, read a graph or table, compare data, or choose a conclusion supported by an experiment.

Do not pick an answer only because it sounds scientific. Go back to the prompt. The right answer has to fit the setup, chart, table, observation, or data given in the question.

ATI TEAS Science Question Formats and Problem Styles

ATI TEAS questions can use standard and alternate item formats across the exam. On NursingMocks, answer using the format shown in the Science set rather than assuming every set uses the same question type.

The bigger difference is the problem style. One Science question may test direct recall. Another may ask you to connect structure and function, interpret a scenario, read a diagram, compare data, or judge whether a conclusion follows from an experiment.

How Science Practice Works on NursingMocks

Open a Science set, read each prompt closely, and answer from the information provided. When you finish, check the correct answers and review explanations when they are included.

Do not rush the review. A score tells you what happened, but the missed questions tell you why. If several misses come from the same content area or the same kind of prompt, that is the clue for your next practice session.

Timed ATI TEAS Science Practice

The official Science section allows 60 minutes for 50 questions, which averages about 1.2 minutes per question. That average is useful, but Science does not feel evenly timed.

Some questions are quick if you know the fact. Others slow you down because they include a scenario, chart, experiment, or unfamiliar wording. Do not burn too much time trying to rescue one hard question while easier points are still available.

Review Your Science Answers, Explanations, and Results

Do not put every missed Science question in the same bucket. Most misses come from one of four places:

Knowledge gap: You did not know the fact, term, process, or concept.

Relationship error: You knew the parts but misunderstood how they connect.

Prompt interpretation error: You missed a qualifier, scenario detail, or requested outcome.

Evidence error: You misread a chart, table, experiment, observation, or data pattern.

This keeps review practical. If most misses are knowledge gaps, go back to the topic. If the misses are evidence errors, practice more chart, table, and experiment questions. If prompt wording keeps catching you, slow down on words like not, least, except, increase, decrease, before, and after.

This section is not only grammar. Conventions matter, but Knowledge of Language and Vocabulary Acquisition carry almost the same weight, so your practice should include sentence clarity, word meaning, paragraph organization, and revision decisions.

What Is the NursingMocks ATI TEAS English Practice Test?

The NursingMocks ATI TEAS English Practice Test is a subject-focused practice page for students preparing for the English and Language Usage section of the ATI TEAS. It is an independent practice resource, not the official ATI TEAS exam, and it does not provide official ATI questions.

Use it when English feels easy in theory but messy in actual questions. A sentence can look fine at first glance, then hinge on punctuation, agreement, word choice, or whether the revision actually improves the meaning.

What Topics Are Covered on ATI TEAS English and Language Usage?

ATI TEAS English and Language Usage is organized around Conventions of Standard English, Knowledge of Language, and Vocabulary Acquisition. Those areas are connected, but they are not the same task.

For practice, separate the decision you are making. Are you fixing an error? Choosing clearer wording? Understanding a word from context? Organizing a sentence or paragraph so the meaning is easier to follow?

Conventions of Standard English Practice Questions

Conventions questions focus on accepted written English. Practice may involve spelling, punctuation, capitalization where relevant, sentence structure, agreement, and usage.

Small marks matter here. A comma can separate ideas correctly or create confusion. A sentence may sound normal when spoken but still contain a fragment, run-on, or agreement problem in writing.

Knowledge of Language Practice Questions

Knowledge of Language questions focus on how language choices affect clarity, tone, purpose, and organization. You may need to choose the sentence that is clearest, the wording that fits the audience, or the revision that improves a paragraph.

Do not choose the longest option just because it sounds more formal. TEAS English often rewards clean, direct wording. If an answer adds clutter without improving meaning, be suspicious.

Vocabulary Acquisition Practice Questions

Vocabulary Acquisition questions focus on word meaning. You may need to use context clues, prefixes, suffixes, roots, or nearby sentence meaning to decide which word or phrase fits best.

The trap is choosing a word you recognize instead of the word the sentence actually needs. Slow down around answer choices that are close in meaning but different in tone, precision, or grammatical fit.

ATI TEAS English Question Formats and Problem Styles

ATI TEAS questions can use standard and alternate item formats across the exam. On NursingMocks, answer using the format shown in the English set instead of assuming every set works the same way.

The more important difference is the English decision being tested. One question may ask you to fix punctuation. Another may ask which sentence improves clarity, which word fits the context, or which revision makes a paragraph more logical.

How English Practice Works on NursingMocks

Open an English set, read the sentence or short prompt carefully, and answer based on the wording provided. When you finish, check the correct answers and review explanations when they are included.

Do not rush past the explanation. The score tells you how many you missed, but the explanation helps you see the pattern. A repeated punctuation miss needs different review than a vocabulary miss or a paragraph-organization miss.

Timed ATI TEAS English Practice

The official English and Language Usage section allows 37 minutes for 37 questions, which averages about one minute per question. That sounds simple until a revision question makes you compare several answers that all look possible.

Move quickly on direct convention questions when the error is clear. Save more attention for questions involving tone, paragraph flow, or word meaning in context. Watch for prompt words such as best, most clearly, not, least, except, before, and after.

Review Your English Answers, Explanations, and Results

Do not treat every missed English question as a grammar problem. Most misses come from one of four places:

  • Convention error: You missed a spelling, punctuation, sentence-structure, capitalization, or usage convention.

  • Meaning and context error: You misunderstood the sentence meaning, a qualifier, or the relationship between ideas.

  • Audience and purpose error: You chose wording that did not fit the intended tone, reader, or reason for writing.

  • Revision and organization error: You chose an option that did not make the sentence or paragraph clearer, tighter, or better organized.

This makes review more useful. If convention errors repeat, review the rule and practice similar questions. If revision errors repeat, compare the answer choices for clarity, concision, and logical flow instead of relying on which option sounds familiar.

Start ATI TEAS English Practice

Start with one NursingMocks English set and let the results show what needs attention. Grammar may be part of the score, but English practice also asks you to notice meaning, word choice, sentence flow, and revision quality.
